title: Users, Stakeholders and the Landscape Around Your Design
objectives: Create effective stakeholder maps for government architecture projects
Apply power/interest grids to prioritise stakeholder engagement
Distinguish between user needs and stakeholder wants
Understand GDS user research principles and their architecture implications
Manage competing demands from multiple stakeholder groups
Navigate the political landscape that shapes architecture decisions
whyThisMatters:
No architecture exists in a vacuum. Every solution you design sits within a landscape of people — users who depend on it, stakeholders who fund it, teams who build it, operators who run it, and leaders who are accountable for it. If you design without understanding this landscape, you'll produce something that's technically elegant but organisationally undeliverable. You'll miss requirements that nobody thought to tell you about. You'll make enemies of people who should be allies.

In UK government, the stakeholder landscape is uniquely complex. You're not working for a single product owner with clear authority. You're navigating policy teams, operational teams, security teams, commercial teams, GDS assessors, ministerial private offices, and sometimes other departments entirely. Each has legitimate interests, different priorities, and varying levels of influence. The architect who can map this landscape, understand the dynamics, and navigate them skilfully will deliver better solutions than the architect who focuses only on the technology.

content.heading: Why Stakeholder Understanding Is an Architecture Skill
content.body:
Many architects treat stakeholder management as someone else's job — the delivery manager's, the business analyst's, the programme manager's. This is a mistake that leads to architecture failures.

Consider what happens when an architect doesn't understand their stakeholders. They design a solution that meets the requirements as written, but the requirements were written by one stakeholder group and don't reflect the needs of others. The security team discovers the design doesn't meet their standards — three months into development. The operations team realises they can't support the proposed architecture — after it's been built. The ministerial private office learns the service can't produce the reports the minister needs — at launch.

Every one of these failures is an architecture failure, not a project management failure. The architect should have identified these stakeholders, understood their needs, and designed a solution that accommodated them. Not perfectly — trade-offs are inevitable — but consciously, with the trade-offs made explicit and agreed.

Stakeholder understanding is an architecture skill because architecture decisions affect people, and people affect architecture decisions. The security team's requirements shape your technology choices. The operations team's capabilities constrain your deployment model. The policy team's future plans influence your extensibility decisions. The minister's priorities determine your timeline and scope. If you don't understand these influences, you're designing blind.

In the DDaT framework, stakeholder understanding is explicitly called out as a capability for Solution Architects. At senior levels, you're expected not just to manage stakeholders but to influence them — helping them understand the implications of their requirements and guiding them toward decisions that serve the whole system, not just their individual interests.

content.heading: Stakeholder Mapping for Government Architecture
content.body:
Stakeholder mapping is the foundation of stakeholder management. In government, the stakeholder landscape is broader and more complex than in most private sector contexts. Here's how to map it effectively.

**Start with the obvious stakeholders:** The programme sponsor or SRO, the delivery team, the policy team, the end users. These are the people everyone thinks of.

**Then add the governance stakeholders:** GDS assessors (if the service is public-facing), departmental architecture review boards, information asset owners, senior information risk owners (SIROs), data protection officers. These people have formal authority to approve or block your architecture.

**Then add the operational stakeholders:** The team that will run the service in production, the service desk that will handle user queries, the incident management team, the change management board. These people will live with your architecture decisions long after the project team has moved on.

**Then add the adjacent stakeholders:** Teams that own systems you need to integrate with, teams that own data you need to access, teams in other departments who might be affected by or interested in your work, commercial teams who manage relevant vendor contracts.

**Finally, add the political stakeholders:** The minister's private office, parliamentary question teams, press office, and any external bodies (regulators, auditors, select committees) who might scrutinise the service.

For each stakeholder, capture:
- **Name and role** — be specific, not generic
- **Interest** — what do they care about in relation to your architecture?
- **Influence** — how much power do they have to shape or block decisions?
- **Current attitude** — are they supportive, neutral, or resistant?
- **Engagement approach** — how and how often will you engage with them?
- **Key concerns** — what keeps them up at night about this project?

A common mistake is creating a stakeholder map once and filing it away. Stakeholder landscapes change. People move roles. Priorities shift. New stakeholders emerge as the project progresses. Review and update your stakeholder map regularly — at least monthly, and whenever there's a significant change in the project or organisation.

content.heading: The Power/Interest Grid in Practice
content.body:
The power/interest grid is a simple but powerful tool for prioritising stakeholder engagement. Plot each stakeholder on two axes: their power (ability to influence or block your architecture decisions) and their interest (how much they care about the outcome).

**High Power, High Interest — Manage Closely:** These are your key stakeholders. In government, this typically includes the SRO, the policy lead, and the departmental SIRO (for services handling sensitive data). You need regular, substantive engagement with these people. They need to understand your architecture decisions and the trade-offs involved. If they're surprised by something, you've failed.

**High Power, Low Interest — Keep Satisfied:** These stakeholders can block you but don't pay close attention unless something goes wrong. In government, this often includes the departmental CTO, GDS spend control teams, and ministerial private offices. Your engagement strategy is to keep them informed at a high level and ensure nothing reaches them as a surprise. A quarterly update or a brief before key decision points is usually sufficient.

**Low Power, High Interest — Keep Informed:** These stakeholders care deeply but can't directly influence decisions. In government, this often includes operational staff, end users, and junior members of the delivery team. They deserve to be heard — their insights are valuable — but you don't need their approval for every decision. Regular updates and opportunities to provide input are appropriate.

**Low Power, Low Interest — Monitor:** These stakeholders are peripherally connected to your work. Keep an eye on them in case their power or interest changes, but don't invest significant engagement effort.

The grid has limitations. In government, power dynamics are fluid. A stakeholder with low formal power can suddenly become critical if a minister asks them a question, if a Freedom of Information request arrives, or if an incident occurs. The grid is a planning tool, not a fixed map.

Also, be careful about dismissing 'low power' stakeholders. The caseworker who processes applications daily may have low organisational power but high knowledge power. Ignoring their input because they're not senior enough is a classic architecture mistake. Some of the best architecture insights come from the people closest to the actual work.

content.heading: User Needs vs Stakeholder Wants: The Critical Distinction
content.body:
The GDS Service Standard is built on a fundamental principle: start with user needs. This sounds simple. In practice, it creates one of the most challenging dynamics an architect faces — the tension between what users need and what stakeholders want.

User needs are observable. They emerge from research — watching people try to complete tasks, listening to their frustrations, understanding their context. A user need might be: 'I need to report my building's energy performance data without having to understand complex technical classifications.'

Stakeholder wants are aspirational. They emerge from organisational priorities, political pressures, and personal preferences. A stakeholder want might be: 'I want a comprehensive data platform that captures every possible data point about building energy performance, with real-time analytics and machine learning predictions.'

Both are legitimate inputs to architecture. But they're not equal. User needs define what the service must do to be useful. Stakeholder wants define what the organisation would like the service to do. When they conflict — and they will — user needs should generally win.

This is easier said than done. The stakeholder who wants the comprehensive data platform is often more senior, more vocal, and more politically connected than the users who just want to submit their data and get on with their day. Standing firm on user needs in the face of stakeholder pressure requires evidence, courage, and diplomacy.

The architect's role is to make this tension visible and help resolve it constructively. Present the user research evidence. Show what happens when user needs are ignored (poor adoption, workarounds, complaints, failed assessments). Propose solutions that meet user needs while accommodating stakeholder wants where possible. And be honest when a stakeholder want would compromise the user experience — 'We can add those 15 extra data fields, but our research shows that every additional field reduces completion rates by 3%. Do we want to accept that trade-off?'

The best architects find creative solutions that serve both users and stakeholders. The worst architects either ignore users (building what stakeholders want) or ignore stakeholders (building what users need but can't get organisational support for). Neither approach succeeds.

content.heading: GDS User Research Principles and Architecture Implications
content.body:
The Government Digital Service has established user research principles that directly affect how architects work. Understanding these principles helps you design architectures that support good user experiences rather than undermining them.

**'Start with user needs, not government needs.'** This means your architecture should be shaped by how users need to interact with the service, not by how the department wants to organise its data. If users think in terms of 'my application' but the department thinks in terms of 'cases,' your architecture needs to bridge that gap — presenting a user-centric view while maintaining the departmental data model underneath.

**'Design for the whole journey, not just the digital part.'** Users don't experience your architecture — they experience a service that might include digital interactions, phone calls, letters, face-to-face meetings, and waiting. Your architecture needs to support this whole journey. That means integration with contact centre systems, letter generation, appointment booking, and status tracking across channels. An architecture that only handles the online form is an incomplete architecture.

**'Make things accessible and inclusive.'** Accessibility isn't a feature — it's a constraint that shapes architecture decisions. Your architecture needs to support WCAG 2.2 AA compliance, which means considering how content is structured, how forms are built, how errors are communicated, and how the service works with assistive technologies. This has real architecture implications — for example, a single-page application architecture might create accessibility challenges that a traditional multi-page approach avoids.

**'Iterate based on evidence.'** Your architecture needs to support iteration. That means designing for changeability — modular components, clear interfaces, feature flags, and deployment pipelines that allow frequent, low-risk releases. An architecture that requires a six-month release cycle to make changes is incompatible with evidence-based iteration.

**'Be inclusive, open and honest.'** Your architecture documentation should be understandable by non-technical stakeholders. Your design decisions should be transparent and defensible. Your assessment of risks and trade-offs should be honest, even when the truth is uncomfortable.

These principles aren't abstract ideals. They have concrete architecture implications that you need to consider from the earliest stages of design. An architect who treats user research as 'someone else's problem' will consistently produce architectures that fail at assessment and frustrate users.

content.heading: Managing Competing Demands: The Art of Architecture Negotiation
content.body:
In government, competing demands are the norm, not the exception. Policy wants maximum data collection. Users want minimum effort. Security wants maximum control. Delivery wants maximum speed. Operations wants maximum simplicity. Finance wants minimum cost. Your job is to find the architecture that best balances these competing demands — and to make the trade-offs explicit.

Here's a framework for managing competing demands:

**1. Make the demands visible.** Create a simple table showing each stakeholder group, what they want, and why. When competing demands are written down side by side, the conflicts become obvious — and so do the potential compromises.

**2. Identify the non-negotiables.** Some demands are genuinely non-negotiable: legal requirements, security classifications, accessibility standards. These are constraints, not preferences. Separate them from the negotiable demands.

**3. Quantify the trade-offs.** Don't just say 'there's a trade-off between security and usability.' Quantify it: 'Adding two-factor authentication will increase security but our research shows it will reduce completion rates by 15% for users over 65. Here are three approaches with different security/usability balances.'

**4. Propose options, not ultimatums.** Present stakeholders with options that represent different balances of their competing demands. Let them choose, with full understanding of the consequences. This is more effective than the architect making the choice unilaterally.

**5. Document the decisions.** When a trade-off is agreed, document it. Who decided? What was the rationale? What was traded off? This protects everyone — including you — when someone later asks 'why does the service work this way?'

**6. Revisit regularly.** The balance of competing demands shifts over time. A security concern that was low priority becomes critical after a data breach in another department. A usability issue that was accepted becomes unacceptable when adoption rates disappoint. Build in regular reviews of your trade-off decisions.

The architect who tries to satisfy everyone satisfies no one. The architect who makes trade-offs explicit and helps stakeholders make informed choices earns trust and delivers better outcomes. This is one of the most important — and least taught — skills in solution architecture.

content.heading: Understanding the Political Landscape
content.body:
Government architecture operates within a political landscape that shapes decisions in ways that have no parallel in the private sector. Ignoring this landscape doesn't make it go away — it just means you'll be blindsided by it.

**Ministerial priorities** drive timelines and scope. When a minister announces a service at a conference, the launch date becomes a political commitment. Your architecture needs to accommodate this reality. That might mean designing for a phased launch — core functionality by the political deadline, full functionality later — rather than insisting on a technically ideal timeline.

**Spending reviews and budget cycles** constrain your options. Government budgets are allocated annually and reviewed periodically. A multi-year programme might lose funding mid-way through. Your architecture should be designed so that each phase delivers usable value, not just technical foundations that only become useful when the whole programme is complete.

**Cross-departmental dynamics** affect integration and data sharing. Departments have different priorities, different technology stacks, and sometimes different political masters. A data sharing initiative that makes perfect technical sense might be blocked by departmental politics. Understanding these dynamics helps you design architectures that work within political reality.

**Public scrutiny** means your decisions must be defensible. Freedom of Information requests, National Audit Office reviews, Public Accounts Committee hearings, and media coverage can all shine a light on architecture decisions. 'We chose this expensive approach because the architect liked the technology' is not a defensible position. 'We chose this approach because it best balanced user needs, security requirements, and value for money, as documented in our options appraisal' is.

**The election cycle** creates uncertainty. A change of government can change policy direction overnight. Architectures that are tightly coupled to specific policy implementations are vulnerable. Architectures that separate policy rules from technical infrastructure are more resilient.

None of this means you should become a political operator. It means you should be politically aware — understanding the forces that shape your operating environment and designing architectures that are robust within that environment. The best government architects combine technical excellence with political literacy. They know when to push back and when to adapt, when to insist on the right approach and when to find a pragmatic compromise.

content.heading: Building Your Stakeholder Engagement Practice
content.body:
Stakeholder engagement isn't a one-off activity — it's an ongoing practice that you develop throughout a project and throughout your career.

**Start every engagement by listening.** Before you present your architecture, understand what the stakeholder cares about. Ask open questions: 'What's your biggest concern about this programme?' 'What would success look like from your perspective?' 'What's worked well or badly on similar projects?' The answers will tell you how to frame your architecture in terms that resonate with them.

**Tailor your communication.** The same architecture decision needs to be communicated differently to different audiences. For the SRO: focus on risk, cost, and timeline implications. For the security team: focus on threat mitigation and compliance. For the delivery team: focus on technical approach and implementation considerations. For the minister's private office: focus on user impact and political messaging. This isn't being manipulative — it's being effective.

**Build relationships before you need them.** Don't wait until you need the security team's approval to introduce yourself. Engage early, build rapport, and understand their perspective before you're in a position where you need their sign-off. People are more likely to support an architecture they've been involved in shaping than one that's presented to them as a fait accompli.

**Be honest about bad news.** If your architecture has a weakness, say so before someone else discovers it. If a timeline is unrealistic, say so early rather than late. If a stakeholder's requirement can't be met within the constraints, explain why and propose alternatives. Honesty builds trust, and trust is the currency of stakeholder relationships.

**Keep a stakeholder journal.** After each significant stakeholder interaction, note what you learned, what concerns were raised, and what you committed to. This helps you track the evolving stakeholder landscape and ensures you follow through on commitments. Broken promises destroy stakeholder relationships faster than anything else.

**Know when to escalate.** Sometimes stakeholder conflicts can't be resolved at your level. When two senior stakeholders have genuinely incompatible requirements and neither will compromise, escalate to the SRO or programme board with a clear description of the conflict, the options, and the trade-offs. Don't try to resolve political conflicts through technical cleverness — it rarely works and often makes things worse.

workedExample.title: ICS Digital Service with Conflicting Stakeholder Needs
workedExample.context:
ICS Digital is building a new grants management service for DESNZ that will handle applications for the Industrial Energy Transformation Fund (IETF). The service needs to allow businesses to apply for grants to fund energy efficiency improvements in industrial processes. The SA has identified the following stakeholders with conflicting needs:

- **Policy team:** Wants to collect extensive data about each application to inform future policy development (30+ data fields per application)
- **Operations team:** Wants a simple, streamlined process they can manage with their current team of 8 caseworkers
- **Security team:** Wants enhanced identity verification for all applicants because the grants involve significant public funds (up to £30m per award)
- **Ministerial private office:** Wants real-time dashboards showing fund allocation by region and sector for parliamentary questions
workedExample.approach:
The SA maps the stakeholders and their competing demands, then works through the conflicts systematically.

**Conflict 1: Data collection scope (Policy vs Users vs Operations)**
Policy wants 30+ fields. User research shows completion rates drop significantly after 15 fields. Operations can't process complex applications quickly enough. The SA proposes a phased approach: collect essential data (12 fields) at application, then gather additional policy-relevant data during the assessment process when caseworkers are already in dialogue with applicants. This satisfies policy's data needs without burdening users or overwhelming operations.

**Conflict 2: Identity verification (Security vs User experience)**
Security wants Companies House verification, director identity checks, and financial standing confirmation before an application can be submitted. This would create a multi-day onboarding process that deters legitimate applicants. The SA proposes risk-based verification: basic checks at application (Companies House number validation, email verification), enhanced checks only for applications that pass initial assessment and are being considered for funding. This focuses the expensive verification on the 20% of applications that proceed, not the 100% that apply.

**Conflict 3: Real-time dashboards (Private office vs Delivery timeline)**
Real-time dashboards require event-driven architecture and a separate reporting data store — adding 6-8 weeks to the timeline. The SA proposes a pragmatic alternative: daily batch reporting for the first release (data refreshed overnight), with real-time capability added in a subsequent phase. For parliamentary questions, a daily refresh is sufficient — PQs have a response deadline of days, not minutes.

**Resolution approach:**
The SA presents all three conflicts to the programme board with options for each, clearly showing the trade-offs. The board makes informed decisions, and the SA documents each decision as an Architecture Decision Record.
workedExample.outcome: The service launches on time with a design that balances all stakeholder needs through pragmatic compromise. Application completion rates are 78% (above the 70% target), caseworkers can process applications within their capacity, security is proportionate to risk, and the private office gets the reporting they need. The policy team gets their additional data through the assessment process rather than the application form. No stakeholder got everything they wanted, but every stakeholder's core need was met.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The SA's value was in making the conflicts visible and quantifiable. Before the SA's analysis, each stakeholder group was advocating for their requirements independently, unaware of the impact on other groups. By presenting the trade-offs clearly — 'every additional field reduces completion by 3%' — the SA enabled informed decision-making rather than the loudest-voice-wins dynamic that often prevails in government programmes.

civilServiceScenario.title: Navigating a Cross-Departmental Stakeholder Minefield
civilServiceScenario.background: DESNZ is leading a new initiative to create a single digital service for businesses to report their carbon emissions across multiple regulatory frameworks. Currently, businesses report similar data to DESNZ (for climate change agreements), the Environment Agency (for pollution prevention), and HMRC (for the climate change levy). The initiative has support from all three departments at director level, but the working-level teams have significant concerns.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: Each department has different data requirements, different reporting periods, different verification processes, and different IT systems. The Environment Agency's team is concerned about losing control of their data quality processes. HMRC's team is worried about the security implications of sharing tax-related data. DESNZ's policy team wants to use the consolidated data for new analytical purposes that weren't part of the original scope. Meanwhile, the business users just want to stop reporting the same information three times.
constraints: Three departments with different governance structures and approval processes
Different data standards and reporting periods across departments
HMRC data has special handling requirements due to taxpayer confidentiality
Environment Agency has statutory obligations for data quality that can't be compromised
Business users have been promised a simpler reporting experience
No single department has authority over the others
Budget is shared across departments with no clear ownership of overruns
Each department has different technology platforms and security accreditations
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect for this cross-departmental initiative, employed by ICS Digital but working across all three departments. You report to a joint programme board with representatives from each department.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests your ability to navigate a complex stakeholder landscape where no single authority can resolve conflicts. You need to build trust with three different technical teams, each of whom may see you as an outsider. You need to find architecture patterns that respect each department's constraints while delivering the simplified experience promised to businesses.

Key architecture decisions will include: whether to build a single system or a federated model with a common front-end; how to handle HMRC's data confidentiality requirements; how to reconcile different data standards; and how to manage the different reporting periods. Each decision will have stakeholders on both sides.

The SA's approach should be to start with what everyone agrees on (businesses shouldn't have to report the same data three times), build trust through small wins (perhaps a shared data dictionary or a common validation service), and tackle the hardest problems (HMRC data sharing, governance model) once relationships are established.

practiceArtefact.description: For the cross-departmental carbon emissions reporting scenario, produce: (1) A comprehensive stakeholder map identifying all stakeholders across the three departments, their interests, power levels, and current attitudes. (2) An engagement strategy for your first month that builds trust and surfaces the key conflicts early.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Think beyond the obvious technical stakeholders. Consider legal teams (data sharing agreements), commercial teams (existing vendor contracts), communications teams (business-facing messaging), and parliamentary teams (who may need to answer questions about the initiative). For the engagement strategy, consider the order in which you engage stakeholders — who do you need onside first to build momentum?
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Stakeholder Map:**

| Stakeholder | Department | Interest | Power | Attitude | Engagement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Joint Programme Board | All | Delivery, value for money | Very High | Supportive | Fortnightly board meetings |
| DESNZ Policy Lead | DESNZ | Data for policy analysis | High | Enthusiastic | Weekly 1:1 |
| EA Data Quality Manager | EA | Maintaining data standards | High | Cautious | Weekly 1:1, involve in design |
| HMRC Security Lead | HMRC | Taxpayer data protection | Very High | Resistant | Early, frequent engagement |
| DESNZ Tech Lead | DESNZ | Integration with existing systems | Medium | Supportive | Architecture working group |
| EA Tech Lead | EA | Minimal disruption to current systems | Medium | Neutral | Architecture working group |
| HMRC Tech Lead | HMRC | Security compliance | High | Cautious | Architecture working group |
| Business representative group | External | Simpler reporting | Low (formal) | Supportive | Monthly user research |
| DPOs (x3) | All | GDPR compliance, data sharing | High | Neutral | Early DPIA engagement |
| Legal teams (x3) | All | Data sharing agreements | High | Process-focused | Early engagement on legal framework |
| GDS assessors | Central | Service Standard compliance | Medium | Neutral | Pre-assessment briefing |

**First Month Engagement Strategy:**

Week 1: Individual meetings with each department's tech lead. Listen to their concerns, understand their current systems, and identify quick wins. Don't propose solutions yet.

Week 2: Meet HMRC security lead — the most resistant stakeholder. Acknowledge their concerns explicitly. Ask them to help define the security requirements rather than presenting a design for them to approve. This gives them ownership.

Week 3: Joint workshop with all three tech leads to map the data landscape — what data is collected by each department, where it overlaps, and where it differs. Produce a shared data dictionary as the first tangible output.

Week 4: Present initial findings to the programme board. Be honest about the challenges (especially HMRC data sharing) and propose a phased approach that delivers early value while the harder problems are worked through.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a project where a stakeholder conflict wasn't resolved well. What was the impact on the architecture? What would you do differently?
How do you currently balance user needs against stakeholder wants? Do you have a consistent approach, or does it vary by project?
When was the last time you were surprised by a stakeholder you hadn't identified? What did you learn from that experience?
How politically aware are you in your current role? Can you identify the political dynamics that affect your architecture decisions?
How do you handle a situation where a senior stakeholder's requirement would harm the user experience? What's your approach?

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is stakeholder understanding considered an architecture skill rather than a project management skill?
options: Because architects are more senior than project managers
Because architecture decisions affect stakeholders and stakeholder requirements shape architecture decisions
Because the DDaT framework requires architects to manage stakeholders
Because project managers don't have time for stakeholder management
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architecture decisions directly affect stakeholders (security choices affect users, deployment choices affect operations teams), and stakeholder requirements directly shape architecture decisions. This bidirectional relationship makes stakeholder understanding a core architecture skill, not just a project management concern.

knowledgeCheck.question: On a power/interest grid, how should you engage with stakeholders who have high power but low interest?
options: Ignore them — they're not interested so they won't interfere
Engage them intensively to increase their interest
Keep them satisfied with high-level updates and ensure no surprises reach them
Treat them the same as high power, high interest stakeholders
knowledgeCheck.explanation: High power, low interest stakeholders (like departmental CTOs or GDS spend control teams) can block your work if they're surprised or dissatisfied, but they don't need detailed involvement. Keep them informed at a high level and ensure nothing reaches them as an unwelcome surprise.

knowledgeCheck.question: When user needs conflict with a senior stakeholder's requirements, what should the architect do?
options: Always prioritise the senior stakeholder's requirements — they have more authority
Always prioritise user needs — the Service Standard requires it
Present the evidence for user needs, quantify the trade-offs, and help stakeholders make an informed decision
Escalate immediately to the programme board without attempting resolution
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The architect's role is to make the conflict visible, present evidence (especially user research), quantify the trade-offs, and help stakeholders make informed decisions. While user needs should generally take priority (per the Service Standard), the architect facilitates the decision rather than making it unilaterally.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the political landscape matters for architecture decisions?
options: Ministerial announcements can create fixed delivery deadlines
Budget cycles constrain multi-year programme funding
Architects should design solutions that favour the current government's policies
Public scrutiny means architecture decisions must be defensible
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architects should design solutions that are politically aware but politically neutral. Designing to favour a specific government's policies would make the architecture vulnerable to policy changes. The other options — ministerial deadlines, budget cycles, and public scrutiny — are legitimate political factors that architects must consider.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective way to resolve competing stakeholder demands in a government architecture context?
options: Let the most senior stakeholder's requirements take priority
Find a technical solution that satisfies all demands equally
Make the competing demands visible, quantify the trade-offs, and present options for informed decision-making
Escalate all conflicts to the SRO for resolution
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Making conflicts visible and quantifying trade-offs enables informed decision-making. This is more effective than defaulting to hierarchy (which ignores important perspectives), seeking perfect compromise (which is often impossible), or escalating everything (which overwhelms senior leaders and abdicates your responsibility as architect).

practicalExercise.title: Stakeholder Conflict Resolution Workshop
practicalExercise.scenario:
You're the SA for a new DESNZ digital service that will allow energy companies to submit compliance data for the Emissions Trading Scheme. You've identified four key stakeholder groups with conflicting requirements:

1. **Policy team:** Wants quarterly reporting with 45 data fields to support detailed policy analysis
2. **Energy companies (users):** Want annual reporting with minimal data fields — they already report similar data to Ofgem
3. **Compliance team:** Wants real-time data submission so they can identify non-compliance early
4. **IT operations:** Wants to minimise integration complexity — they're already supporting 12 other services with a small team
practicalExercise.task:
1. Create a conflict matrix showing where these four groups' requirements clash
2. For each conflict, propose a compromise that partially satisfies both sides
3. Identify which conflicts can be resolved through architecture design and which require a governance decision
4. Write a one-page brief for the programme board that presents the key trade-offs and your recommended approach
hints: Consider whether the reporting frequency conflict could be resolved with a phased approach
Think about whether the data field conflict could be resolved by separating mandatory and optional fields
Consider whether Ofgem data could be reused to reduce the burden on energy companies
Think about what 'real-time' actually means to the compliance team — do they need sub-second or same-day?
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**Conflict Matrix:**

| Conflict | Groups | Nature | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reporting frequency | Policy (quarterly) vs Users (annual) vs Compliance (real-time) | Fundamental — affects architecture pattern | High |
| Data scope | Policy (45 fields) vs Users (minimal) | Significant — affects user experience and data model | High |
| Integration complexity | Compliance (real-time feeds) vs IT Ops (minimal integration) | Moderate — affects technical approach | Medium |
| Data source | Users (new submission) vs Potential Ofgem reuse | Opportunity — could reduce all conflicts | Medium |

**Proposed Compromises:**

1. **Frequency:** Quarterly submission (satisfying policy) with a simple online form that auto-saves progress (reducing user burden). 'Real-time' for compliance reframed as 'within 24 hours of submission' — which quarterly submission achieves. Compliance gets early warning through automated validation checks at submission time.

2. **Data scope:** 15 mandatory fields at submission (core compliance data), 30 optional fields that policy can request during assessment. Investigate Ofgem data reuse to pre-populate fields, reducing user effort.

3. **Integration:** Batch integration (overnight) rather than real-time APIs, reducing IT ops burden. Compliance dashboard refreshed daily from the batch data.

**Architecture vs Governance Decisions:**
- Architecture can resolve: integration pattern (batch vs real-time), data model (mandatory vs optional fields), Ofgem data reuse approach
- Governance must resolve: reporting frequency (quarterly vs annual — this is a policy decision), minimum data requirements (what's legally required vs nice-to-have)

**Programme Board Brief:**
The key trade-off is between data richness (which policy needs for analysis) and user simplicity (which drives compliance rates). Our recommended approach: quarterly submission of 15 mandatory fields via a simple online service, with optional additional fields and Ofgem data reuse to enrich the dataset without burdening users. This gives policy 80% of the data they need with 40% of the user burden. We recommend a governance decision on whether the remaining 20% of policy data justifies the additional user friction of making more fields mandatory.
assessmentCriteria: Conflict matrix clearly identifies the competing requirements and their severity
Compromises are creative and practical, not just splitting the difference
Clear distinction between architecture decisions and governance decisions
Programme board brief is concise, honest about trade-offs, and includes a clear recommendation

commonMistakes: Treating stakeholder management as someone else's responsibility and focusing only on technical design
Creating a stakeholder map once and never updating it as the project evolves
Defaulting to the most senior stakeholder's requirements without considering other perspectives
Ignoring operational stakeholders who will live with the architecture long after the project team moves on
Failing to quantify trade-offs — saying 'there's a trade-off' without showing the specific impact of each option
Treating all stakeholders equally rather than prioritising engagement based on power and interest
Ignoring the political landscape and being blindsided by ministerial priorities or budget changes
Presenting architecture decisions as purely technical when they have significant stakeholder implications

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA designs the Emissions Trading Scheme service based solely on the policy team's requirements — they're the 'customer,' after all. The service collects 45 data fields quarterly with real-time integration to the compliance system. It's technically sophisticated but has a 35% completion rate because energy companies find it burdensome. The IT operations team struggles to support the real-time integration alongside their other services. The compliance team discovers that 'real-time' data that's 65% incomplete is less useful than complete data delivered quarterly. The service fails its beta assessment because user needs weren't adequately considered.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA maps all stakeholders, surfaces the conflicts, and facilitates informed trade-offs. They discover that Ofgem already holds 60% of the required data, reducing the burden on energy companies. They propose quarterly submission of 15 mandatory fields with optional enrichment, and daily batch reporting for compliance. The service achieves a 82% completion rate, the operations team can support it sustainably, and the compliance team gets reliable, complete data. The policy team gets less data than they originally wanted but more than they would have got from a service with a 35% completion rate.
